questions.questionText: What is displacement?
questions.hint: Displacement is a vector quantity.

questions.questionText: Velocity is the rate of change of:
questions.hint: Velocity tells how quickly position changes.

questions.questionText: Acceleration is the rate of change of:
questions.hint: Acceleration tells how quickly velocity changes.

questions.questionText: A car travels 120 m in 6 s. What is its average speed?
questions.hint: Average speed = distance ÷ time.

questions.questionText: A runner has a displacement of 50 m east in 10 s. What is the average velocity?
questions.hint: Average velocity = displacement ÷ time.

questions.questionText: A car changes velocity from 0 m/s to 20 m/s in 5 s. What is its acceleration?
questions.hint: a = (v - u) ÷ t.

questions.questionText: A bicycle speeds up from 4 m/s to 12 m/s in 4 s. What is its acceleration?
questions.hint: a = (v - u) ÷ t.

questions.questionText: A car slows down from 30 m/s to 10 m/s in 5 s. What is its acceleration?
questions.hint: a = (v - u) ÷ t. Slowing down gives negative acceleration if forward is positive.

questions.questionText: Which equation can be used to find final velocity?
questions.hint: Use this equation when you know initial velocity, acceleration, and time.

questions.questionText: An object starts from rest and accelerates at 3 m/s² for 4 s. What is its final velocity?
questions.hint: Use v = u + at. Rest means u = 0.

questions.questionText: A car has an initial velocity of 5 m/s and accelerates at 2 m/s² for 6 s. What is its final velocity?
questions.hint: v = u + at.

questions.questionText: An object starts from rest and accelerates at 2 m/s² for 5 s. What is its displacement?
questions.hint: Use s = ut + ½at². Rest means u = 0.

questions.questionText: A car moves with an initial velocity of 4 m/s, acceleration of 2 m/s², for 3 s. What is its displacement?
questions.hint: Use s = ut + ½at².

questions.questionText: Which equation is useful when time is not given?
questions.hint: This equation does not include time.

questions.questionText: A ball starts from rest and accelerates at 2 m/s² over 9 m. What is its final velocity?
questions.hint: Use v² = u² + 2as.

questions.questionText: A car speeds up uniformly from 10 m/s to 20 m/s in 4 s. What is its displacement?
questions.hint: Use s = ((u + v) / 2)t.

questions.questionText: A ball is launched horizontally. If air resistance is ignored, its horizontal velocity is:
questions.hint: Gravity acts vertically, not horizontally.

questions.questionText: A projectile has a horizontal velocity of 8 m/s and flies for 3 s. What is its horizontal displacement?
questions.hint: Horizontal displacement = horizontal velocity × time.

questions.questionText: A ball is dropped from rest. Ignoring air resistance, what is its velocity after 2 s? Use g = 10 m/s².
questions.hint: Use v = u + gt. Dropped from rest means u = 0.

questions.questionText: Fluid resistance usually causes a projectile to have:
questions.hint: Fluid resistance opposes motion and reduces range.
choices: Greater range than without air resistance
Smaller range than without air resistance

questions.questionText: Newton's First Law states that an object will remain at rest or move at constant velocity unless:
questions.hint: Newton's First Law is also called the law of inertia.
choices: A resultant external force acts on it

questions.questionText: Newton's Second Law is represented by:
questions.hint: Force depends on mass and acceleration.

questions.questionText: Newton's Third Law states that:
questions.hint: Forces come in pairs.
choices: Every action has an equal and opposite reaction

questions.questionText: A 5 kg object accelerates at 2 m/s². What is the resultant force?
questions.hint: Use F = ma.

questions.questionText: A 4 kg cart experiences a resultant force of 20 N. What is its acceleration?
questions.hint: Rearrange F = ma to a = F/m.

questions.questionText: A free-body diagram is used to show:
questions.hint: Free-body diagrams represent forces using arrows.
choices: The chemical formula of an object
The forces acting on an object

questions.questionText: If two forces of 10 N and 6 N act in the same direction, what is the resultant force?
questions.hint: Forces in the same direction are added.

questions.questionText: If a 15 N force acts right and a 5 N force acts left, what is the resultant force?
questions.hint: Opposite forces are subtracted.

questions.questionText: Linear momentum is calculated using:
questions.hint: Momentum depends on mass and velocity.

questions.questionText: A 2 kg object moves at 3 m/s. What is its momentum?
questions.hint: Use p = mv.

questions.questionText: A 10 kg object has a momentum of 50 kg m/s. What is its velocity?
questions.hint: Rearrange p = mv to v = p/m.

questions.questionText: Momentum remains constant in a system unless:
questions.hint: External forces can change total momentum.
choices: The system is closed and no external force acts
A resultant external force acts on the system

questions.questionText: Impulse is calculated using:
questions.hint: Impulse depends on force and contact time.

questions.questionText: A force of 20 N acts for 3 s. What is the impulse?
questions.hint: Use J = FΔt.

questions.questionText: Impulse is equal to:
questions.hint: J = Δp.

questions.questionText: An object's momentum changes from 10 kg m/s to 25 kg m/s. What is the impulse?
questions.hint: Impulse = final momentum - initial momentum.

questions.questionText: In an elastic collision, which quantities are conserved?
questions.hint: Elastic collisions conserve both.

questions.questionText: In an inelastic collision, which quantity is always conserved if no external force acts?
questions.hint: Momentum is conserved in closed systems.

questions.questionText: Centripetal acceleration is directed:
questions.hint: Centripetal means center-seeking.
choices: Toward the center of the circle

questions.questionText: A body moves in a circle at constant speed. What changes?
questions.hint: Velocity is a vector, so changing direction means velocity changes.

questions.questionText: Centripetal acceleration can be calculated using:
questions.hint: Use this formula when speed and radius are given.

questions.questionText: A car moves in a circle at 10 m/s with radius 5 m. What is its centripetal acceleration?
questions.hint: Use a = v²/r.

questions.questionText: Centripetal force acts:
questions.hint: Centripetal force changes direction, not necessarily speed.
choices: Perpendicular to the velocity and toward the center

questions.questionText: The relationship between linear speed and angular velocity is:
questions.hint: Linear speed depends on angular velocity and radius.

questions.questionText: An object has angular velocity 4 rad/s and radius 2 m. What is its linear speed?
questions.hint: Use v = ωr.

questions.questionText: The principle of conservation of energy states that energy:
questions.hint: Energy changes form, but the total amount is conserved.
choices: Can be created but not destroyed
Can be destroyed but not created
Cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred or transformed

questions.questionText: Work done by a force is equivalent to:
questions.hint: When work is done, energy is transferred.

questions.questionText: Which equation calculates work done by a constant force at an angle?
questions.hint: Only the component of force in the direction of displacement does work.

questions.questionText: A force of 10 N moves an object 5 m in the same direction as the force. How much work is done?
questions.hint: Use W = Fs when θ = 0°, so cos 0° = 1.

questions.questionText: A 20 N force moves an object 3 m in the direction of the force. How much work is done?
questions.hint: Work = force × displacement.

questions.questionText: If a force is perpendicular to displacement, the work done is:
Mechanical energy is the sum of:
questions.hint: Mechanical energy includes motion energy and stored mechanical energy.
choices: Kinetic energy, gravitational potential energy, and elastic potential energy
Heat energy and sound energy only
Chemical energy and nuclear energy only

questions.questionText: The equation for kinetic energy is:
questions.hint: Kinetic energy depends on mass and the square of velocity.

questions.questionText: A 2 kg object moves at 4 m/s. What is its kinetic energy?
questions.hint: Use Eₖ = ½mv².

questions.questionText: A 10 kg object moves at 2 m/s. What is its kinetic energy?
questions.hint: Eₖ = ½mv².

questions.questionText: The change in gravitational potential energy near Earth is calculated using:
questions.hint: Gravitational potential energy depends on mass, gravity, and height.

questions.questionText: A 2 kg object is lifted 5 m. Use g = 10 m/s². What is the increase in gravitational potential energy?
questions.hint: Use ΔEₚ = mgΔh.

questions.questionText: A 3 kg object is raised 4 m. Use g = 10 m/s². What is its gain in gravitational potential energy?
questions.hint: Multiply mass × gravity × height.

questions.questionText: The equation for elastic potential energy is:
questions.hint: Elastic potential energy is stored in stretched or compressed objects.

questions.questionText: A spring has k = 100 N/m and is stretched by 0.20 m. What is the elastic potential energy?
questions.hint: Use Eₕ = ½k(Δx)².

questions.questionText: Power is defined as:
questions.hint: Power tells how fast work is done.
choices: The rate of doing work or transferring energy
The total force on an object
The amount of mass in a system

questions.questionText: Which equation calculates power from work and time?
questions.hint: Power = work done ÷ time taken.

questions.questionText: A machine does 200 J of work in 10 s. What is its power?
questions.hint: Use P = W/t.

questions.questionText: A force of 50 N moves an object at 2 m/s in the direction of the force. What power is developed?
questions.hint: Use P = Fv.

questions.questionText: Efficiency can be calculated using:
questions.hint: Efficiency compares useful output energy to input energy.

questions.questionText: A device receives 100 J of input energy and produces 80 J of useful output energy. What is its efficiency?
questions.hint: Efficiency = output energy ÷ input energy × 100.

questions.questionText: A motor has an input power of 500 W and useful output power of 400 W. What is its efficiency?
questions.hint: Efficiency = output power ÷ input power × 100.

questions.questionText: A Sankey diagram is used to represent:
questions.hint: Sankey diagrams show where energy goes.

questions.questionText: Energy density describes:
questions.hint: Fuels with high energy density store more energy in less mass or volume.
choices: The amount of energy stored per unit mass or volume
The acceleration of a falling object

questions.questionText: According to molecular theory, particles in a solid:
questions.hint: In solids, particles are close together and vibrate in place.

questions.questionText: Particles in a gas usually:
questions.hint: Gas particles move randomly and spread out.
choices: Move freely and are far apart

questions.questionText: Density is calculated using:
questions.hint: Density is mass divided by volume.

questions.questionText: An object has a mass of 20 g and a volume of 5 cm³. What is its density?
questions.hint: Use ρ = m/V.

questions.questionText: A liquid has a mass of 60 g and a volume of 20 mL. What is its density?
questions.hint: Divide mass by volume.

questions.questionText: Temperature in science can be measured using:
questions.hint: Kelvin and Celsius are temperature scales.

questions.questionText: The Kelvin scale is important because it measures temperature from:
questions.hint: Absolute zero is 0 K.

questions.questionText: A temperature change of 10°C is equal to a temperature change of:
questions.hint: Temperature changes are the same size in Celsius and Kelvin.

questions.questionText: Kelvin temperature is a measure of the average:
questions.hint: Higher temperature means particles move faster on average.

questions.questionText: Internal energy is the total:
questions.hint: Internal energy includes particle motion and particle interactions.
choices: Random kinetic energy and intermolecular potential energy of particles
Mass and volume of the system

questions.questionText: Thermal energy naturally transfers from:
questions.hint: Temperature difference determines the direction of thermal energy transfer.
choices: Smaller objects to larger objects only
Denser objects to lighter objects only

questions.questionText: During a phase change, temperature usually:
questions.hint: Energy is used to change state, not temperature.
choices: Stays constant while energy changes particle behavior

questions.questionText: Which equation is used to calculate thermal energy transfer when temperature changes?
questions.hint: Use Q = mcΔT when there is a temperature change.

questions.questionText: How much energy is needed to heat 2 kg of water by 5°C if c = 4200 J/kg°C?
questions.hint: Use Q = mcΔT.

questions.questionText: A 1 kg object with c = 500 J/kg°C is heated by 4°C. How much energy is transferred?
questions.hint: Q = mcΔT.

questions.questionText: Which equation is used during a phase change?
questions.hint: Use Q = mL when temperature stays constant during a phase change.

questions.questionText: How much energy is needed to melt 2 kg of a substance if L = 100,000 J/kg?
questions.hint: Use Q = mL.

questions.questionText: The three main mechanisms of thermal energy transfer are:
questions.hint: Heat can transfer through direct contact, fluid movement, or electromagnetic waves.

questions.questionText: Conduction happens mainly because particles:
questions.hint: Conduction happens through particle interactions.

questions.questionText: In the conduction equation ΔQ/Δt = kA(ΔT/Δx), increasing the area A will:
questions.hint: A larger area allows more thermal energy to transfer per second.
choices: Decrease the rate of heat transfer
Increase the rate of heat transfer

questions.questionText: Convection happens in fluids because:
questions.hint: Fluids include liquids and gases.
choices: Density differences cause warmer and cooler fluid to move

questions.questionText: Thermal radiation transfers energy by:
questions.hint: Radiation can travel through empty space.

questions.questionText: The Stefan-Boltzmann law for luminosity is:
questions.hint: Luminosity depends strongly on absolute temperature.

questions.questionText: Apparent brightness depends on luminosity and:
questions.hint: A source appears dimmer when it is farther away.

questions.questionText: Wien's displacement law relates peak wavelength to:
questions.hint: Hotter objects emit peak radiation at shorter wavelengths.

questions.questionText: The greenhouse effect is related to conservation of energy because energy:
questions.hint: Energy is not created or destroyed, but it can be transferred or transformed.
choices: Is absorbed, reflected, emitted, or transferred

questions.questionText: The greenhouse effect helps keep Earth:
questions.hint: Greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit infrared radiation.
choices: Warmer than it would be without greenhouse gases

questions.questionText: Which gas is a greenhouse gas?
questions.hint: CO₂ absorbs infrared radiation.

questions.questionText: Which list contains only greenhouse gases?
questions.hint: Greenhouse gases include carbon dioxide, methane, water vapor, and nitrous oxide.

questions.questionText: Emissivity compares the radiation emitted by a surface to:
questions.hint: An ideal black body is a perfect emitter.
choices: The radiation emitted by an ideal black body at the same temperature

questions.questionText: An ideal black body has an emissivity of:
questions.hint: A perfect emitter has emissivity equal to 1.

questions.questionText: If a surface radiates 300 W/m² and an ideal black body at the same temperature radiates 600 W/m², what is its emissivity?
questions.hint: Emissivity = radiated power per unit area ÷ ideal black body power per unit area.

questions.questionText: If emissivity is 0.80 and an ideal black body radiates 500 W/m², how much power per unit area does the surface radiate?
questions.hint: Surface radiation = emissivity × ideal black body radiation.

questions.questionText: Albedo measures how much incoming radiation is:
questions.hint: High albedo means more radiation is reflected.

questions.questionText: The formula for albedo is:
questions.hint: Albedo compares reflected energy to incoming energy.
choices: Total scattered power ÷ total incident power
Total incident power ÷ total scattered power

questions.questionText: If a surface receives 1000 W and reflects 300 W, what is its albedo?
questions.hint: Albedo = reflected power ÷ incoming power.

questions.questionText: A surface has an albedo of 0.60. If 800 W is incident on it, how much power is reflected?
questions.hint: Reflected power = albedo × incident power.

questions.questionText: Earth’s albedo changes because of:
questions.hint: Clouds and surface type affect reflection.

questions.questionText: The solar constant S represents:
questions.hint: Solar constant is related to incoming solar radiation.
choices: The incoming solar power per unit area near Earth

questions.questionText: Because Earth is a sphere, the mean incoming solar intensity is:
questions.hint: The incoming radiation is spread over Earth’s spherical surface.

questions.questionText: Greenhouse gases mainly absorb:
questions.hint: Earth emits much of its energy as infrared radiation.

questions.questionText: Greenhouse gases absorb infrared radiation because their molecules have:
questions.hint: Molecular vibrations and rotations can absorb infrared energy.
choices: Energy levels that can interact with infrared radiation

questions.questionText: After absorbing infrared radiation, greenhouse gases:
questions.hint: Some emitted radiation returns toward Earth’s surface.

questions.questionText: The enhanced greenhouse effect is caused mainly by:
questions.hint: Burning fossil fuels and agriculture can increase greenhouse gases.
choices: Human activities increasing greenhouse gas concentrations

questions.questionText: Methane has the chemical formula:
questions.hint: Methane contains carbon and hydrogen.

questions.questionText: Pressure is defined as:
questions.hint: Use P = F/A.

questions.questionText: A force of 100 N acts perpendicular to an area of 5 m². What is the pressure?
questions.hint: Use P = F/A.

questions.questionText: A pressure of 50 Pa acts on an area of 4 m². What force is applied?
questions.hint: Rearrange P = F/A to F = PA.

questions.questionText: The amount of substance n can be calculated using:
questions.hint: N is the number of molecules and NA is Avogadro’s constant.

questions.questionText: Avogadro’s constant represents:
questions.hint: One mole contains about 6.02 × 10²³ particles.
choices: The number of particles in one mole

questions.questionText: If a sample contains 6.02 × 10²³ molecules, how many moles are present?
questions.hint: 6.02 × 10²³ particles = 1 mol.

questions.questionText: An ideal gas is:
questions.hint: Ideal gases are simplified models.
choices: A model used to approximate the behavior of real gases
A gas that has no temperature
A gas made only of oxygen
A gas that cannot exert pressure

questions.questionText: According to kinetic theory, gas pressure is caused by:
questions.hint: Collisions with surfaces create pressure.
choices: Gas particles colliding with the container walls

questions.questionText: Which equation is the ideal gas law?
questions.hint: The ideal gas law connects pressure, volume, amount of gas, and temperature.

questions.questionText: In the equation PV = nRT, what does T represent?
questions.hint: Gas law temperature must be in kelvin.

questions.questionText: In the equation PV = nRT, what does n represent?
questions.hint: n is measured in mol.

questions.questionText: For a fixed amount of gas, which quantity stays constant in the combined gas law?
questions.hint: The combined gas law can be written as PV/T = constant.

questions.questionText: If temperature is constant, what happens to pressure when volume decreases?
questions.hint: At constant temperature, pressure and volume are inversely related.

questions.questionText: A gas has a pressure of 100 kPa and volume of 2 L. If the volume decreases to 1 L at constant temperature, what is the new pressure?
questions.hint: Use P₁V₁ = P₂V₂.

questions.questionText: If pressure is constant, what happens to volume when temperature increases?
questions.hint: At constant pressure, volume and kelvin temperature are directly related.

questions.questionText: If volume is constant, what happens to pressure when temperature increases?
questions.hint: At constant volume, pressure and kelvin temperature are directly related.

questions.questionText: A gas has n = 2 mol, R = 8.31 J/mol K, and T = 300 K. What is the value of PV?
questions.hint: From PV = nRT, multiply nRT.

questions.questionText: The internal energy of an ideal monatomic gas is given by:
questions.hint: For a monatomic ideal gas, U depends on amount of gas and temperature.

questions.questionText: For a monatomic ideal gas with n = 2 mol, R = 8.31 J/mol K, and T = 100 K, what is the internal energy?
questions.hint: Use U = 3/2 nRT.

questions.questionText: A real gas behaves most like an ideal gas when it has:
questions.hint: Ideal gas behavior is best when particles are far apart and moving fast.

questions.questionText: What do cells provide in a circuit?
questions.hint: A cell provides energy to move charge around a circuit.

questions.questionText: Which device can act as an energy source in a circuit?
questions.hint: Chemical cells convert chemical energy into electrical energy.

questions.questionText: A solar cell converts light energy into:
questions.hint: Solar cells can be used as energy sources in circuits.

questions.questionText: Circuit diagrams are used to represent:
questions.hint: Circuit diagrams use symbols to show how components are connected.

questions.questionText: Direct current, or dc current, is:
questions.hint: Direct current flows in one direction around a circuit.
choices: A flow of charge carriers in one direction
A force acting on a magnet

questions.questionText: Current is calculated using:
questions.hint: Current is charge flow per unit time.

questions.questionText: If 12 C of charge flows past a point in 3 s, what is the current?
questions.hint: Use I = Δq/Δt.

questions.questionText: If a current of 2 A flows for 5 s, how much charge passes through the circuit?
questions.hint: Rearrange I = Δq/Δt to Δq = IΔt.

questions.questionText: If 20 C of charge flows in 4 s, what is the current?
questions.hint: Current = charge ÷ time.

questions.questionText: Ohm's law is:
questions.hint: Ohm's law connects voltage, current, and resistance.

questions.questionText: A resistor has a current of 2 A and a resistance of 3 Ω. What is the voltage?
questions.hint: Use V = IR.

questions.questionText: A 12 V battery is connected to a 4 Ω resistor. What is the current?
questions.hint: Rearrange V = IR to I = V/R.

questions.questionText: A resistor has a voltage of 10 V and current of 2 A. What is its resistance?
questions.hint: Rearrange V = IR to R = V/I.

questions.questionText: In a series circuit, the current is:
questions.hint: Series circuits have only one path for current.

questions.questionText: In a series circuit, total resistance is found by:
questions.hint: For series resistors, Rₛ = R₁ + R₂ + ...

questions.questionText: Two resistors of 3 Ω and 5 Ω are connected in series. What is the total resistance?
questions.hint: Add resistances in series.

questions.questionText: In a series circuit, the total voltage is:
questions.hint: In series, V = V₁ + V₂ + ...
choices: The sum of the voltages across each component
Equal to only the smallest voltage

questions.questionText: A series circuit has voltage drops of 4 V and 6 V. What is the total voltage?
questions.hint: Add the voltage drops in a series circuit.

questions.questionText: In a parallel circuit, components are connected in:
questions.hint: Parallel circuits allow current to split.

questions.questionText: In a parallel circuit, the voltage across each branch is:
questions.hint: Parallel branches share the same potential difference.

questions.questionText: Two identical resistors are connected in parallel. Compared with one resistor alone, the total resistance is:
questions.hint: Adding parallel branches gives current more paths.

questions.questionText: Which component is used to measure current?
questions.hint: An ammeter is connected in series to measure current.

questions.questionText: Which component is used to measure voltage?
questions.hint: A voltmeter is connected in parallel across a component.

questions.questionText: A resistor is used to:
questions.hint: Higher resistance makes it harder for charge to flow.

questions.questionText: For current to flow, a circuit must be:
questions.hint: Charges need a complete path to move.
